screens.title: Introduction to Amazon EC2
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we introduce Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, or EC2, which provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. EC2 lets you rent virtual servers called instances: you pick a machine image, an instance type, storage and network settings, and you launch the instance on demand. That flexibility means you only pay for what you run, and you can scale from a single development server to many instances behind a load balancer. You will learn what an AMI is, how instance types differ by family and size, and why selecting the right instance family matters for cost and performance. We also cover practical security basics: security groups as a virtual firewall, key pairs for SSH access, and common mistakes such as leaving SSH open to the world. Finally, you will see how EC2 ties into EBS for persistent storage, Elastic Load Balancing for distribution, and Auto Scaling Groups for resilience. By the end you will understand the core parts of launching and securing an EC2 web server and how EC2 fits into larger AWS architectures. Think about a simple website you would deploy: which AMI, instance family, and security rules would you choose, and why?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what EC2 is and why it is central to many AWS architectures, differentiate the common instance families and select an appropriate instance type for a workload, and configure and launch an instance using AMIs, key pairs, and security groups. You will also practice core security best practices: restricting SSH or RDP access to known IPs, protecting private key files, and using EBS for persistent block storage. Each objective links knowledge to practice: for example, knowing instance families lets you choose a compute-optimized family for C P U-heavy batch jobs instead of overpaying for memory-optimized instances. Knowing how to configure a security group prevents a common mistake—leaving SSH and RDP open to the internet. These objectives prepare you to design resilient, cost-effective architectures and to safely run a basic web server on EC2 as a hands-on exercise. Consider which objective you want to practice first: launching an instance, securing it, or choosing the right instance family.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical focus
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives screen focuses on practical skills and security habits you will adopt. You will configure and launch an EC2 instance from an AMI, create and secure a key pair for SSH access, and define security group rules that permit only necessary traffic. The hands-on activity shows how to pick Amazon Linux 2 as the AMI and t2. micro as the instance type for a low-cost web server, then create a security group that allows HTTP from anywhere but SSH only from your IP. You will also practice cleanup steps to avoid charges and lingering open security groups. These practical objectives prepare you to perform the lab confidently and to reason about decisions when architecting production systems. As you work, ask yourself which default choices could become security risks and how you would mitigate them.

screens.title: What is EC2 and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. At its core, EC2 gives you virtual servers called instances that run operating systems and applications you choose. The instance lifecycle starts with an AMI — an Amazon Machine Image — which is a template containing the OS, application server, and any preinstalled software. Launching an instance from an AMI creates a running virtual server you can access and manage like a physical machine. For example, you might launch an Amazon Linux 2 AMI and then install a web server to host a small site. The advantage over physical servers is speed and flexibility: you can create standardized AMIs to reproduce environments and scale by launching more instances when demand rises. A common misconception is treating EC2 like a single monolithic product; instead, it's a set of constructs—AMIs, instance types, storage, networking, and security—that you assemble. This means an EC2-based architecture can range from a single development instance to a fleet behind a load balancer with auto scaling. When planning, think about the required OS, preinstalled software, and whether you should bake those into a custom AMI for repeatable deployments. How would you standardize a web server image for your team?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › What is EC2 and why it matters
Definition
EC2 provides resizable compute capacity through virtual servers called instances. AMIs are templates that define the software configuration for an instance.
Analogy
Think of AMIs as appliance blueprints and instances as the running appliances you start from the blueprint.
Concrete example
Choose an Amazon Linux 2 AMI and launch a t2.micro for a low-cost development web server.
Key takeaway
Use AMIs to standardize deployments and speed up provisioning across environments.
Details & common misconception
  • Instances are ephemeral by default; persistent state should live on EBS volumes unless baked into an AMI.
  • AMIs can be public, marketplace, or custom; baking configuration into an AMI improves reproducibility.
  • Misconception: an AMI equals a running server. It is a template, not the active running state.
Key Takeaway

Use AMIs to create repeatable server images and launch instances on demand to scale capacity.

screens.title: EC2 instance types and families
screens.narratorSegment: Instance types are standardized combinations of C P U, memory, storage, and network capacity, grouped into families. The most important families are General Purpose, Compute Optimized, Memory Optimized, Storage Optimized, and Accelerated Computing. General Purpose instances such as t3 and m5 provide a balance of resources and are suitable for web servers and small databases; for example, t3. micro is a burstable general-purpose instance often used for development and low-traffic sites. Compute Optimized instances like the c6g family are designed for C P U-bound workloads—batch processing or high-performance web servers—that need more C P U relative to memory. Memory Optimized instances are for in-memory databases and large caches; Storage Optimized instances provide high local input and output for workloads needing fast disk throughput. Accelerated Computing instances include GPUs or FPGAs for machine learning or graphics. A common mistake is choosing a memory-optimized instance for a C P U-bound app, which wastes money. When selecting an instance, profile your workload: if C P U utilization is the bottleneck, prefer compute-optimized; if memory limits performance, choose memory-optimized. Consider cost, performance, and the possibility of using Auto Scaling to handle peaks without oversizing single instances. Which family would you pick for a nightly C P U-bound batch job?

keyIdea.title: Match family to workload
keyIdea.text: Pick an instance family based on CPU, memory, storage, and network needs to optimize cost and performance.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › EC2 instance types and families
Families at a glance
General Purpose (t3, m5)
Balanced CPU/memory; good default for web servers and small DBs.
Compute Optimized (c6g)
High CPU per core for batch processing and compute-heavy apps.
Memory Optimized (r6g)
Large RAM for in-memory databases and analytics.
Storage Optimized (i3)
High local I/O for databases requiring fast disk throughput.
Decision checklist
  • Identify the workload bottleneck: CPU, memory, or I/O.
  • Choose the family that addresses that bottleneck to avoid overpaying.
  • Use burstable instances for low-traffic workloads and scaling for spikes.
Key Takeaway

Base your choice on measured bottlenecks; selecting the wrong family wastes cost without improving performance.

screens.title: VPCs, subnets, and placement
screens.narratorSegment: Every EC2 instance runs inside a Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, which is a logically isolated network you control. Within a VPC you create subnets, which partition the network into segments—often public subnets for internet-facing resources and private subnets for internal services. Launching an instance into a public subnet that has a route to an internet gateway lets that instance receive traffic from the internet, assuming its security group allows it. In contrast, instances in a private subnet have no direct internet route unless you use a NAT gateway or proxy. Understanding placement matters because it affects accessibility and security: put web servers that must serve public traffic in public subnets while placing databases in private subnets. A common misconception is that security groups alone fully isolate resources; network-level design using VPCs and subnets is equally important. When you design, think about which instances require public IPs, which should be private, and whether to use multiple Availability Zones for high availability. For example, host your load balancer in public subnets and backend instances in private subnets to reduce direct exposure. How would you place a three-tier web application across subnets and zones to balance accessibility and safety?

keyIdea.title: Network placement shapes access
keyIdea.text: VPCs and subnets determine whether instances are internet-facing or private; combine with security groups for layered protection.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › VPCs, subnets, and placement
VPC basics
A VPC is your isolated network. Subnets divide that network; public subnets connect to the internet gateway, private subnets do not.
Public Subnet
Hosts resources with public IPs behind security groups, typically load balancers or bastion hosts.
Private Subnet
Hosts internal services like databases, often without direct internet access.
Design tips
  • Place internet-facing load balancers in public subnets and application servers in private subnets.
  • Use multiple Availability Zones to increase resilience.
  • Remember network design and security groups work together; neither replaces the other.
Key Takeaway

Place public-facing resources in public subnets and keep sensitive services in private subnets to limit exposure.

screens.title: Security Groups: virtual firewall rules
screens.narratorSegment: Security groups act as virtual firewalls controlling inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances. They are stateful: if you allow inbound traffic for a connection, the return traffic is allowed automatically. When creating a security group, you define rules by protocol (typically TCP), port range, and source (an IP range or another security group). A typical web server security group allows inbound HTTP and HTTPS from anywhere and SSH only from your specific public IP. A frequent and dangerous mistake is setting SSH or RDP source to 0.0.0.0/0, which permits connection attempts from the entire internet. Instead, restrict administrative ports to known IP addresses and consider using a bastion host or session manager for administrative access. Security groups are applied at the instance level, so you can have different rules for front-end and back-end servers. Remember that overly permissive rules may go unnoticed; treat security group review as a regular practice. As you design rules, ask whether each inbound port is necessary and whether traffic should be limited by IP range or by another security group for tighter control. Security Groups: virtual firewall rules means security groups should allow only necessary traffic; avoid 0.0.0.0/0 for administrative ports and prefer ip-restricted or group-based rules.. In practical terms, define inbound and outbound rules to control instance traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Security Groups: virtual firewall rules
Security Group essentials
Define inbound and outbound rules by protocol, port, and source. Security groups are stateful and applied at the instance level.
Good example
Allow HTTP/HTTPS from 0.0.0.0/0 and SSH from your home office public IP only.
Common mistake
Opening SSH or RDP to 0.0.0.0/0 exposes the instance to broad attack surface.
Checklist
  • Review inbound rules: is each port necessary?
  • Restrict administrative ports to specific IPs or security groups.
  • Use layered controls: network placement, security groups, and IAM for defense in depth.
Key Takeaway

Never leave administrative ports open to all; treat security groups as a first line of defense and review them regularly.

screens.title: Key pairs and secure SSH access
screens.narratorSegment: Key pairs are the standard method for secure SSH access to Linux EC2 instances and are used to decrypt Windows administrator passwords. When you create or select a key pair at launch, AWS stores the public key on the instance and gives you the private key file to keep. The private key authenticates your SSH session. A critical operational step is protecting that private key: store it with restrictive file permissions and never share it. For example, on Mac O S or Linux you would run a permission command to limit access to the file so only you can read it. Losing the private key means you cannot SSH into the instance, and if it is compromised an attacker could gain access. A common misconception is that you can re-download a private key from AWS; you cannot. If you lose the key, you must use other recovery techniques or replace the instance. In practice, treat private keys like sensitive credentials: use secure storage, back them up in a safe location, and consider using systems like instance connect or session manager for ephemeral access in production. When you create a key pair, decide who should hold the private key and how access will be rotated and audited.

keyIdea.title: Protect the private key
keyIdea.text: AWS gives the private key once at creation; store it securely, set restricted file permissions, and never share it.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Key pairs and secure SSH access
How key pairs work
AWS stores the public key on the instance. You keep the private key to authenticate via SSH. AWS does not retain your private key after creation.
Permission example
On Linux/macOS, run chmod 400 your-key-pair.pem to restrict the private key file's permissions.
Risks and recovery
  • If the private key is lost, you cannot re-download it from AWS; plan for recovery or replacement.
  • If the private key is compromised, rotate access and consider replacing the instance.
  • Consider alternatives such as session manager for managed, auditable access in production.
Key Takeaway

Treat private keys as sensitive credentials: protect file permissions, avoid sharing, and plan recovery ahead of time.

screens.title: Hands-on: Launching and connecting to a basic EC2 web server
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough follows the hands-on activity steps: choose an AMI, pick an instance type, configure a security group, create a key pair, and connect to the instance to install a web server. In the console you would pick Amazon Linux 2 AMI and a t2. micro for the free-tier eligible example. Create a security group named web-server-sg that allows HTTP from anywhere and SSH only from your public IP. When launching, choose Create a new key pair, download the. pem file, and save it securely. Once the instance is running, use the private key to SSH into the public DNS. On a terminal you first restrict key permissions with a permission command, then connect by specifying the private key and the ec2-user account. After connecting, update packages, install the Apache httpd server, start and enable it, and write a simple index. html. The chapter provides example commands; use them as shown to verify your setup. A common error on connection is missing the SSH inbound rule in the security group—verify that rule and your public IP. After the lab, remember to terminate the instance and delete the security group and key pair to avoid charges and exposure. Which verification step would you run first if SSH fails?

keyIdea.title: Practical verification
keyIdea.text: Follow the lab steps and use the SSH permission and install commands to verify a running web server; always clean up afterward.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Hands-on: Launching and connecting
Starter commands (visual)
Use these commands once you've downloaded your key and identified the instance public DNS or IP.
chmod 400 /path/to/my-web-key.pem
ssh -i /path/to/my-web-key.pem ec2-user@<Your_Instance_Public_DNS_or_IP>
# once connected
sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install -y httpd
sudo systemctl start httpd
sudo systemctl enable httpd
echo "<h1>Hello from my AWS EC2 Web Server!</h1>" | sudo tee /var/www/html/index.html
If you cannot connect, verify the security group's inbound SSH rule allows your public IP and that the instance is in running state.
Example verification
Open your browser to the instance Public IPv4 or DNS to see the Hello message after installing the web server. If you see it, networking and the web server are configured correctly.
Cleanup reminder

Terminate your EC2 instance and remove the security group and key pair to avoid charges and lingering exposure.

screens.title: EBS, ELB, and Auto Scaling integration
screens.narratorSegment: EC2 instances provide compute but rely on other services for persistent storage, traffic distribution, and resilience. Elastic Block Store, or EBS, supplies persistent block storage that you attach to instances—think of it like a virtual hard drive that survives instance restarts when used with appropriate volume types. For high availability and to distribute traffic, Elastic Load Balancing sits in front of multiple instances and evenly routes requests, providing a single endpoint for clients. Auto Scaling Groups connect with load balancers to automatically add or remove instances based on demand or health checks. Together these services form a typical scalable architecture: instances run your application code, EBS holds persistent data, ELB balances traffic across instances, and ASG adjusts capacity to meet load. A common misconception is relying on a single instance with EBS for resilience; a single instance remains a single point of failure. Instead, use multiple instances across Availability Zones with a load balancer and ASG to maintain availability. When designing, ensure your application stores state where it is shared or persistent—EBS volumes are not automatically shared across instances—so prefer shared storage or databases for multi-instance state. How would you ensure session data remains available when instances scale out?

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Several recurring mistakes appear when learners first use EC2. The most common security error is leaving SSH or RDP open to the internet by setting the security group source to 0.0.0.0/0. This invites scanner traffic and increases risk. Avoid this by restricting the source to your public IP or using a bastion host. Another frequent issue is losing the private key: AWS does not allow re-downloading a private key, so if you lose it you cannot SSH into the instance. Protect the private key with restricted file permissions and secure storage. A third mistake is choosing the wrong instance family—like picking a memory-optimized instance for a C P U-bound workload—which unnecessarily raises cost without improving performance. Profile the workload and choose the family accordingly. Finally, leaving test instances running or orphaned security groups can lead to unexpected charges and exposure. Adopt a cleanup habit: terminate test instances, remove unused key pairs, and delete security groups you no longer need. Each of these mistakes has simple mitigations: tighten security group rules, protect keys, measure before choosing instance types, and routinely clean up resources. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we introduce Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud, or EC2, which provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. EC2 lets you rent virtual servers called instances: you pick a machine image, an instance type, storage and network settings, and you launch the instance on demand. That flexibility means you only pay for what you run, and you can scale from a single development server to many instances behind a load balancer. You will learn what an AMI is, how instance types differ by family and size, and why selecting the right instance family matters for cost and performance. We also cover practical security basics: security groups as a virtual firewall, key pairs for SSH access, and common mistakes such as leaving SSH open to the world. Finally, you will see how EC2 ties into EBS for persistent storage, Elastic Load Balancing for distribution, and Auto Scaling Groups for resilience. By the end you will understand the core parts of launching and securing an EC2 web server and how EC2 fits into larger AWS architectures. Think about a simple website you would deploy: which AMI, instance family, and security rules would you choose, and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what EC2 is and why it is central to many AWS architectures, differentiate the common instance families and select an appropriate instance type for a workload, and configure and launch an instance using AMIs, key pairs, and security groups. You will also practice core security best practices: restricting SSH or RDP access to known IPs, protecting private key files, and using EBS for persistent block storage. Each objective links knowledge to practice: for example, knowing instance families lets you choose a compute-optimized family for C P U-heavy batch jobs instead of overpaying for memory-optimized instances. Knowing how to configure a security group prevents a common mistake—leaving SSH and RDP open to the internet. These objectives prepare you to design resilient, cost-effective architectures and to safely run a basic web server on EC2 as a hands-on exercise. Consider which objective you want to practice first: launching an instance, securing it, or choosing the right instance family.

This second objectives screen focuses on practical skills and security habits you will adopt. You will configure and launch an EC2 instance from an AMI, create and secure a key pair for SSH access, and define security group rules that permit only necessary traffic. The hands-on activity shows how to pick Amazon Linux 2 as the AMI and t2. micro as the instance type for a low-cost web server, then create a security group that allows HTTP from anywhere but SSH only from your IP. The why is important: restricting access minimizes attack surface, and storing the private key with tight file permissions prevents accidental compromise. You will also practice cleanup steps to avoid charges and lingering open security groups. These practical objectives prepare you to perform the lab confidently and to reason about decisions when architecting production systems. As you work, ask yourself which default choices could become security risks and how you would mitigate them.

EC2 is a web service that provides resizable compute capacity in the cloud. At its core, EC2 gives you virtual servers called instances that run operating systems and applications you choose. The instance lifecycle starts with an AMI — an Amazon Machine Image — which is a template containing the OS, application server, and any preinstalled software. Launching an instance from an AMI creates a running virtual server you can access and manage like a physical machine. For example, you might launch an Amazon Linux 2 AMI and then install a web server to host a small site. The advantage over physical servers is speed and flexibility: you can create standardized AMIs to reproduce environments and scale by launching more instances when demand rises. A common misconception is treating EC2 like a single monolithic product; instead, it's a set of constructs—AMIs, instance types, storage, networking, and security—that you assemble. This means an EC2-based architecture can range from a single development instance to a fleet behind a load balancer with auto scaling. When planning, think about the required OS, preinstalled software, and whether you should bake those into a custom AMI for repeatable deployments. How would you standardize a web server image for your team?

Instance types are standardized combinations of C P U, memory, storage, and network capacity, grouped into families. The most important families are General Purpose, Compute Optimized, Memory Optimized, Storage Optimized, and Accelerated Computing. General Purpose instances such as t3 and m5 provide a balance of resources and are suitable for web servers and small databases; for example, t3. micro is a burstable general-purpose instance often used for development and low-traffic sites. Compute Optimized instances like the c6g family are designed for C P U-bound workloads—batch processing or high-performance web servers—that need more C P U relative to memory. Memory Optimized instances are for in-memory databases and large caches; Storage Optimized instances provide high local input and output for workloads needing fast disk throughput. Accelerated Computing instances include GPUs or FPGAs for machine learning or graphics. A common mistake is choosing a memory-optimized instance for a C P U-bound app, which wastes money. When selecting an instance, profile your workload: if C P U utilization is the bottleneck, prefer compute-optimized; if memory limits performance, choose memory-optimized. Consider cost, performance, and the possibility of using Auto Scaling to handle peaks without oversizing single instances. Which family would you pick for a nightly C P U-bound batch job?

Every EC2 instance runs inside a Virtual Private Cloud, or VPC, which is a logically isolated network you control. Within a VPC you create subnets, which partition the network into segments—often public subnets for internet-facing resources and private subnets for internal services. Launching an instance into a public subnet that has a route to an internet gateway lets that instance receive traffic from the internet, assuming its security group allows it. In contrast, instances in a private subnet have no direct internet route unless you use a NAT gateway or proxy. Understanding placement matters because it affects accessibility and security: put web servers that must serve public traffic in public subnets while placing databases in private subnets. A common misconception is that security groups alone fully isolate resources; network-level design using VPCs and subnets is equally important. When you design, think about which instances require public IPs, which should be private, and whether to use multiple Availability Zones for high availability. For example, host your load balancer in public subnets and backend instances in private subnets to reduce direct exposure. How would you place a three-tier web application across subnets and zones to balance accessibility and safety?

Security groups act as virtual firewalls controlling inbound and outbound traffic for EC2 instances. They are stateful: if you allow inbound traffic for a connection, the return traffic is allowed automatically. When creating a security group, you define rules by protocol (typically TCP), port range, and source (an IP range or another security group). A typical web server security group allows inbound HTTP and HTTPS from anywhere and SSH only from your specific public IP. A frequent and dangerous mistake is setting SSH or RDP source to 0.0.0.0/0, which permits connection attempts from the entire internet. Instead, restrict administrative ports to known IP addresses and consider using a bastion host or session manager for administrative access. Security groups are applied at the instance level, so you can have different rules for front-end and back-end servers. Remember that overly permissive rules may go unnoticed; treat security group review as a regular practice. As you design rules, ask whether each inbound port is necessary and whether traffic should be limited by IP range or by another security group for tighter control. Security Groups: virtual firewall rules means security groups should allow only necessary traffic; avoid 0.0.0.0/0 for administrative ports and prefer ip-restricted or group-based rules.. In practical terms, define inbound and outbound rules to control instance traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key pairs are the standard method for secure SSH access to Linux EC2 instances and are used to decrypt Windows administrator passwords. When you create or select a key pair at launch, AWS stores the public key on the instance and gives you the private key file to keep. The private key authenticates your SSH session. A critical operational step is protecting that private key: store it with restrictive file permissions and never share it. For example, on Mac O S or Linux you would run a permission command to limit access to the file so only you can read it. Losing the private key means you cannot SSH into the instance, and if it is compromised an attacker could gain access. A common misconception is that you can re-download a private key from AWS; you cannot. If you lose the key, you must use other recovery techniques or replace the instance. In practice, treat private keys like sensitive credentials: use secure storage, back them up in a safe location, and consider using systems like instance connect or session manager for ephemeral access in production. When you create a key pair, decide who should hold the private key and how access will be rotated and audited.

This walkthrough follows the hands-on activity steps: choose an AMI, pick an instance type, configure a security group, create a key pair, and connect to the instance to install a web server. In the console you would pick Amazon Linux 2 AMI and a t2. micro for the free-tier eligible example. Create a security group named web-server-sg that allows HTTP from anywhere and SSH only from your public IP. When launching, choose Create a new key pair, download the. pem file, and save it securely. Once the instance is running, use the private key to SSH into the public DNS. On a terminal you first restrict key permissions with a permission command, then connect by specifying the private key and the ec2-user account. After connecting, update packages, install the Apache httpd server, start and enable it, and write a simple index. html. The chapter provides example commands; use them as shown to verify your setup. A common error on connection is missing the SSH inbound rule in the security group—verify that rule and your public IP. After the lab, remember to terminate the instance and delete the security group and key pair to avoid charges and exposure. Which verification step would you run first if SSH fails?

EC2 instances provide compute but rely on other services for persistent storage, traffic distribution, and resilience. Elastic Block Store, or EBS, supplies persistent block storage that you attach to instances—think of it like a virtual hard drive that survives instance restarts when used with appropriate volume types. For high availability and to distribute traffic, Elastic Load Balancing sits in front of multiple instances and evenly routes requests, providing a single endpoint for clients. Auto Scaling Groups connect with load balancers to automatically add or remove instances based on demand or health checks. Together these services form a typical scalable architecture: instances run your application code, EBS holds persistent data, ELB balances traffic across instances, and ASG adjusts capacity to meet load. A common misconception is relying on a single instance with EBS for resilience; a single instance remains a single point of failure. Instead, use multiple instances across Availability Zones with a load balancer and ASG to maintain availability. When designing, ensure your application stores state where it is shared or persistent—EBS volumes are not automatically shared across instances—so prefer shared storage or databases for multi-instance state. How would you ensure session data remains available when instances scale out?
